mainTopic: Payment for בושת, the size of רבי יוסי הגלילי's fine, and whether a witness can become a judge
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about paying for בושת, which is measured by the honor of the person who was shamed. רבי עקיבא teaches that even poor Jews count as people of high standing, because they are children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב. In the משנה's story, a man tried to avoid paying 400 זוז by showing that the woman uncovered her own head for a little oil. רבי עקיבא answered that shaming yourself does not free others from paying. The גמרא proves from a case of רבי יהודה נשיאה that רבי יוסי הגלילי's fine is a Tyrian מנה. It then asks whether a judge who saw the act himself may judge it, which leads to the rule of אין עד נעשה דיין. Next it checks whether רבי עקיבא really holds that rule, using his debate with שמעון התימני about the word 'fist'. Finally, a ברייתא about an ox that killed and caused damage raises a question, and רבא begins to answer it on this amud. His answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The general rule: payment depends on the person's honor
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states that payment for בושת is measured by the dignity and standing of the person who was shamed.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the principle: everything is according to the honor of the person.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה sums up the rule for paying for בושת: the amount depends on who was shamed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no fixed price for embarrassing someone. The same act may cost more or less depending on the dignity of the victim. This sets up רבי עקיבא's statement right after it.

phrases.english: This is the principle:
everything is according to his honor.
phrases.notes: He means the honor of the person who was shamed. That decides how much is paid.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל הַכֹּל לְפִי כְּבוֹדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the earlier lists of payments in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Payment for בושת is measured according to the honor of the person who was shamed.

steps.title: Even poor Jews are treated as people of high standing
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא teaches that even poor Jews are valued as if they were wealthy people who lost their money, because of their noble ancestry.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said: Even the poor among the Jewish people are viewed as if they were free people of standing who lost their property, since they are the children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא explains how to apply the rule 'according to his honor' to poor people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think a poor person's honor is worth little, so his בושת payment should be small. רבי עקיבא says no. Every Jew comes from noble family, so a poor person is treated like an important person who simply lost his money.
steps.whyThisMatters: This raises the בושת payment for poor people and shows the basic dignity of every Jew.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said:
Even the poor among the Jewish people,
we view them as though they were
free people of standing who lost their property;
for they are the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אֲפִילּוּ עֲנִיִּים שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule of step 1 to poor people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Poor Jews are valued for בושת as if they were people of high standing who lost their wealth.

steps.title: The man who uncovered a woman's head is ordered to pay 400
steps.stepSummary: A man uncovered a woman's head in the marketplace. רבי עקיבא ordered him to pay 400 זוז, and the man asked for time to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident with a man who uncovered a woman's head in the marketplace. She came before רבי עקיבא, and he ordered the man to pay her 400 זוז. The man said: רבי, give me time. And he gave him time.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה begins a story about רבי עקיבא. This opening sets up the man's trick in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Uncovering a married woman's hair in public was a serious embarrassment. So רבי עקיבא set a large payment. The man's request for time hints that he is planning something.

phrases.english: And there was an incident with one man
who uncovered the head of a woman in the marketplace;
she came before Rabbi Akiva,
and he obligated him to give her
four hundred zuz.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: רַבִּי, תֵּן לִי זְמַן.
phrases.english: He said to him: My teacher, give me time.
And he gave him time.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּאֶחָד שֶׁפָּרַע רֹאשׁ הָאִשָּׁה בַּשּׁוּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real case where רבי עקיבא applied the בושת rules.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Uncovering a woman's head in public earned a payment of 400 זוז.

steps.title: The man tricks the woman into uncovering her own head
steps.stepSummary: The man broke a jug with a tiny amount of oil in front of the woman. She uncovered her own head to use the oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: He waited until she was standing at the entrance of her courtyard and broke a jug in front of her that held about an איסר's worth of oil. She uncovered her head and dabbed her hand in the oil and placed it on her head.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: the man sets a trap to show that the woman herself uncovers her head for almost nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An איסר is a tiny coin, so the oil was worth almost nothing. She uncovered her own head to save that small amount. This gives the man his argument in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: he watched and waited for her

phrases.english: He watched for her until she was standing at the entrance of her courtyard,
and he broke the jug in front of her,
and in it was about an issar's worth of oil.
phrases.notes: An איסר is a tiny coin, so the oil was worth almost nothing.

phrases.english: She uncovered her head,
and she was dabbing her hand in the oil
and placing her hand on her head.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמָרָהּ עוֹמֶדֶת עַל פֶּתַח חֲצֵרָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by describing the man's trap.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The woman uncovered her own head in public to save oil worth only an איסר.

steps.title: The man protests: why should I pay her 400?
steps.stepSummary: The man brought witnesses to רבי עקיבא and argued that a woman who uncovers her head for so little does not deserve 400 זוז.
steps.simpleTranslation: He set up witnesses against her and came before רבי עקיבא. He said to him: To this woman I should give 400 זוז?!
steps.whatsHappening: The man challenges רבי עקיבא's ruling, using witnesses to show that the woman herself does not mind uncovering her head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His argument is built on step 1: payment follows the person's honor. If she uncovers her own head for a tiny bit of oil, he says she shows that this does not really shame her. So, he argues, the 400 זוז payment is too much.

phrases.english: He set up witnesses against her,
and he came before Rabbi Akiva;
he said to him: To this woman I should give
four hundred zuz?!
phrases.notes: This is said in shock. He means she clearly doesn't care, so why should he pay so much?

steps.triggerLanguage: לָזוֹ אֲנִי נוֹתֵן אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת זוּז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the trap from step 4 to attack the ruling in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's ruling that the man must pay 400 זוז.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Payment follows the victim's honor. A woman who uncovers her own head for an איסר's worth of oil shows she is not shamed by it. So she should not get a large payment.
steps.whatToRemember: The man tried to use the rule 'everything according to his honor' against the woman. The next step gives רבי עקיבא's answer.

steps.title: Shaming yourself does not cancel what others owe you
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא rejects the man's argument. A person who harms himself is exempt, but others who harm him must pay. The same is true for cutting down one's own young trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: Your argument means nothing. A person who injures himself is exempt, even though he is not allowed to do it, but others who injure him must pay. Someone who cuts down his own young trees is exempt, even though he is not allowed to, but others who cut them down must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא answers the man's claim from the last step. The woman uncovering her own head does not free him from paying her for shaming her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man argued that she cares so little about her dignity that she deserves no 400 זוז. רבי עקיבא says her dignity is still worth the same. Her own act only means she cannot sue herself. Anyone else who hurts her or shames her must still pay in full.

keyTerms.meaning: He is not permitted (it is forbidden)

steps.whatToRemember: Harming yourself is forbidden but brings no payment. Someone else who harms you must pay, even if you did the same thing to yourself.
steps.confusionAlert: 'פטור' does not mean it is allowed. רבי עקיבא says outright that a person is not allowed to hurt himself. He is only exempt from paying.

phrases.english: He said to him: You have said nothing.
One who injures himself,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי – פָּטוּר;
phrases.english: even though he is not permitted, is exempt;
others who injured him are liable.
And one who cuts down his own saplings,
phrases.notes: Cutting down fruit trees for no reason is forbidden. That is why it says 'not permitted' (דברים 20:19).

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי – פָּטוּר;
phrases.english: even though he is not permitted, is exempt;
others are liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: לֹא אָמַרְתָּ כְּלוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the man's challenge from Step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Draws a line between harming oneself and being harmed by others
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since she shamed herself for a little oil, her dignity is worth little, so he should owe less
steps.terutzMaskana: Self-harm only exempts the person himself. Others still owe the full amount based on the victim's standing.

steps.title: Which kind of מנה did the משנה mean
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי יוסי הגלילי's fine of a מנה is in Tyrian coins or in local coins.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: They asked: Did we learn in the משנה a Tyrian מנה, or a local מנה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion of the משנה. It asks which coins are meant in רבי יוסי הגלילי's fixed fine of a מנה for a blow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מנה is 100 דינרים. The value changes a lot depending on the coins. A local מנה is worth only one eighth of a Tyrian מנה, so the answer makes a big difference to how much the striker pays.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked of them (the Sages)
Tyrian, the full-value coinage of the city of צור
Local or provincial coinage, worth much less

phrases.english: Gemara. A question was asked of them:
phrases.notes: This goes back to the משנה's ruling that רבי יוסי הגלילי says one who strikes his fellow pays a מנה.

phrases.english: Did we learn a Tyrian maneh,
or did we learn a local maneh?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: מָנֶה צוֹרִי תְּנַן, אוֹ מָנֶה מְדִינָה תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's discussion of the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the fixed מנה is paid in Tyrian or local coins

steps.title: A real case before רבי יהודה נשיאה
steps.stepSummary: A man struck another. רבי יהודה נשיאה ruled, based on רבי יוסי הגלילי, that he must pay a Tyrian מנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A certain man struck his fellow. The case came before רבי יהודה נשיאה. He said to the striker: Here am I, here is רבי יוסי הגלילי. Give him a Tyrian מנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real ruling to answer the question about the coins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה נשיאה used רבי יוסי הגלילי's fine of a מנה, and he said 'Tyrian' outright. So the case seems to show that the משנה's מנה means Tyrian coins.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
That a certain man struck his fellow.
He came before Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.
He said to him: Here am I,
here is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili;
give him a Tyrian maneh.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a proof to answer the question in Step 7
steps.raayaObject: That the מנה in the משנה is Tyrian
steps.raayaSupportSource: A case judged by רבי יהודה נשיאה

steps.title: Conclusion: it is a Tyrian מנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes from the case that the משנה means a Tyrian מנה, and agrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this: we learned a Tyrian מנה! Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the lesson from the case and agrees with it. The question about the coins is settled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first 'שמע מינה' suggests the conclusion. The second one agrees with it. The fine for a blow according to רבי יוסי הגלילי is 100 full-value Tyrian דינרים.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it (the proof is accepted)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוסי הגלילי, the fine for a blow is a Tyrian מנה, the full-value coins.

phrases.english: Learn from it: we learned a Tyrian maneh!
Learn from it: yes.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: מָנֶה צוֹרִי תְּנַן! שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the case in Step 8
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה's מנה is a Tyrian מנה

steps.title: What did 'here am I, here is רבי יוסי הגלילי' mean
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי יהודה נשיאה meant by his strange words.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'Here am I, here is רבי יוסי הגלילי'?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא looks more closely at the wording of the case. This question sets up the next step, where one possible reading will be tested.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'here am I' are unclear. Why would the judge point to himself? The גמרא wants to understand them before it moves on.

phrases.english: What is meant by "Here am I,
here is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili"?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״הָא אֲנָא, הָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the wording of the case in Step 8
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of רבי יהודה נשיאה's words 'here am I, here is רבי יוסי הגלילי'

steps.title: If he meant 'I saw you,' then a witness became a judge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests he meant 'I saw you hit him.' It then challenges this, because a witness is not supposed to judge the same case.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say this is what he told him: 'Here am I, who saw you, and here is רבי יוסי הגלילי, who says a Tyrian מנה; go give him a Tyrian מנה.' Does that mean a witness can become a judge?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one reading: 'here am I' means 'I saw you strike him.' Then it attacks that reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this reading, רבי יהודה נשיאה was both the one who saw the blow and the one who judged it. The גמרא is surprised, because that would mean an עד can become a דיין in the same case. So this reading looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion that will be challenged)
Is that to say...? (introduces a surprising result)

steps.confusionAlert: 'אילימא' brings a reading that the גמרא is about to knock down. It is not the גמרא's final answer.

phrases.english: If you say this is what he said to him:
Here am I, who saw you,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי – דְּאָמַר מָנֶה צוֹרִי,
phrases.english: and here is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who says a Tyrian maneh;
go give him a Tyrian maneh.
Is that to say that a witness can become a judge?!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּעֵד נַעֲשֶׂה דַּיָּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an answer to Step 10's question and challenges it
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'here am I' means 'I saw you'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: On that reading the judge was also the witness. That implies an עד can serve as a דיין in the same case, which is surprising.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a סנהדרין that saw a murder
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support the challenge that a witness cannot become a judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: if a סנהדרין saw someone kill a person, some of them become witnesses and some become judges. This is רבי טרפון's view. רבי עקיבא says: they are all witnesses, and a witness cannot become a judge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to back up its challenge from the last step: a witness may not judge the case he saw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא records a מחלוקת about judges who saw a crime. רבי טרפון lets the court split into witnesses and judges. רבי עקיבא says everyone who saw it is only a witness, because a witness cannot become a judge.

keyTerms.meaning: A witness cannot become a judge

phrases.english: But isn't it taught:

phrases.aramaic: סַנְהֶדְרִין שֶׁרָאוּ אֶחָד שֶׁהָרַג אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ –
phrases.english: A Sanhedrin that saw someone kill a person:
some of them become witnesses,
and some of them become judges;
these are the words of Rabbi Tarfon.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: כּוּלָּם עֵדִים הֵם,
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: they are all witnesses,
and a witness cannot become a judge.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind the challenge raised in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that רבי יהודה נשיאה could not have been both witness and judge.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא with the מחלוקת of רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא about a סנהדרין that saw a murder.

steps.title: Even רבי טרפון does not let one person be witness and judge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that even the lenient view, רבי טרפון, only splits the court. He never lets the same person both testify and judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי טרפון only said that some become witnesses and some become judges. He never said that a witness himself becomes a judge!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the lesson from the ברייתא: no one allows the same person to be both witness and judge, so רבי יהודה נשיאה could not have done that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think רבי טרפון is lenient about witnesses who judge. But his leniency only lets different people fill the two jobs. For רבי עקיבא it is forbidden all the more. So the reading 'I saw you hit him' looks impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: He only said this much (and no further)

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן –
phrases.english: Rabbi Tarfon only said
that some of them become witnesses
and some of them become judges;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל עֵד נַעֲשֶׂה דַּיָּין – לָא קָאָמַר!
phrases.english: but that a witness becomes a judge, he did not say!
phrases.notes: That is exactly what רבי יהודה נשיאה would have done if he saw it himself and then ruled.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the point of the ברייתא and aims it at the reading from step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that רבי יהודה נשיאה said 'I saw you hit him' and then judged the case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even the lenient view, רבי טרפון, never lets one person act as both witness and judge. So רבי יהודה נשיאה could not have done so.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about judges who saw it at night
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes away the proof. The ברייתא is about a case where the judges saw the murder at night, when they could not act as a court.
steps.simpleTranslation: That ברייתא is about a case where they saw it at night, when they were not able to act as judges.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the ברייתא's case is different from ours.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At night a court cannot judge, so the judges who saw the murder saw it only as regular witnesses. That is why they cannot later judge it. רבי יהודה נשיאה saw the hitting while he could act as a judge, so he may judge it.

keyTerms.meaning: When that ברייתא was taught (it was about a specific case)
Able to act as a court and judge

steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not reject the rule that a witness cannot become a judge. It only limits that rule to someone who saw the act when he could not judge.

phrases.english: When that was taught,
it was a case where they saw it at night,
when they are not fit to carry out judgment.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The words in square brackets are the corrected wording: 'people able to judge.'

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תַּנְיָא הָהִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 12-13 by limiting the ברייתא to a night-time case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the ברייתא as proof against רבי יהודה נשיאה. The rule itself still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא's judges saw the murder at night, when they could not judge. That is not like a judge who sees something during the day.

steps.title: Another reading: he was only stating his view, and other witnesses testified
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: רבי יהודה נשיאה did not see the hitting. He told the attacker that he follows רבי יוסי הגלילי, and that other witnesses had testified.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say this is what he told him: 'Here I am, and I hold like רבי יוסי הגלילי, who says a Tyrian מנה. And here are witnesses testifying against you. Go give him a Tyrian מנה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different way to read רבי יהודה נשיאה's words, so the problem of a witness judging never comes up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this reading, 'הא אנא' means 'I am someone who follows רבי יוסי הגלילי.' It does not mean 'I saw you.' The testimony came from other witnesses, so רבי יהודה נשיאה was only a judge. The ruling of a Tyrian מנה from step 9 stays the same.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)
A מנה (100 זוז) in Tyrian coins

steps.whatToRemember: Both answers keep the ruling of a Tyrian מנה. They only explain how רבי יהודה נשיאה could rule. Either he saw it while able to judge, or other witnesses testified and he only judged.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: this is what he said to him:

phrases.aramaic: הָא אֲנָא – דִּסְבִירָא לִי כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי,
phrases.english: Here I am, who holds like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili,
who says a Tyrian maneh;
and here are witnesses who testify against you;
go give him a Tyrian maneh.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, הָכִי קָאָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, separate answer to the challenge from steps 11-13 by reading his words differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the wording so that he was never a witness.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'הא אנא' meant 'I saw you hit him,' so he was both witness and judge.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'הא אנא' means 'I follow רבי יוסי הגלילי.' Other witnesses testified, and he only judged.

steps.title: Does רבי עקיבא really hold that a witness cannot judge?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether רבי עקיבא really holds the rule that אין עד נעשה דיין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does רבי עקיבא really hold that a witness cannot become a judge?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is opening a new challenge. It questions the idea that רבי עקיבא holds a witness cannot become a judge. This sets up the ברייתא it is about to bring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in step 12 quoted רבי עקיבא as saying 'a witness cannot become a judge.' Now the גמרא asks whether that is really his view, because another ברייתא, brought next, seems to show him saying the opposite. The question is a contradiction between two sources about רבי עקיבא.

keyTerms.meaning: A witness cannot become a judge in the same case

phrases.english: And does Rabbi Akiva hold
that a witness cannot become a judge?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְסָבַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא דְּאֵין עֵד נַעֲשֶׂה דַּיָּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the view of רבי עקיבא quoted in the ברייתא of step 12, that a witness cannot become a judge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that רבי עקיבא holds אין עד נעשה דיין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A source about רבי עקיבא, brought next, seems to show that he allows a witness to act as a judge.

steps.title: שמעון התימני says the weapon must be available for inspection
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: שמעון התימני learns from the word 'fist' that the court must be able to examine the object used to hit.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is taught in a ברייתא about the פסוק 'And a man strikes his fellow with a stone or with a fist': שמעון התימני says, just as a fist is special because the court and the witnesses can examine it, so too any object that the court and witnesses can examine. This leaves out a case where the object is no longer with the witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to build its challenge. This step lays out the opinion of שמעון התימני, which רבי עקיבא will argue with next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fist stays attached to the attacker, so it can always be brought to court and checked. שמעון התימני says the same must be true for any weapon. If the stone is lost, the court cannot judge whether it was strong enough to hurt, so there is no case.

keyTerms.meaning: The assembly, meaning the court of judges

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a baraita:
"And a man strikes his fellow
with a stone or with a fist" –
Shimon HaTimni says:
Just as a fist is special
in that it is available to the court and to the witnesses,
phrases.notes: A fist is always attached to the attacker, so the judges can check it and the witnesses can point to it.

phrases.english: so too anything that is available to the court and to the witnesses;
excluding a case where it left
the hands of the witnesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source that will be used to challenge the claim about רבי עקיבא.
steps.raayaObject: The challenge that רבי עקיבא allows a witness to become a judge.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with the argument between שמעון התימני and רבי עקיבא about שמות 21:18.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: the court did not see the hitting
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers that the court was not there when the hitting happened, so it relies on witnesses anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: Did he hit him in front of the court, so that they know how hard he hit him and where he hit him, whether on his thigh or on the lobe of his heart?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא argues with שמעון התימני. He says the court never saw the hitting, so it already relies on witnesses, and it can rely on them about the weapon too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge to step 16 comes from these words. רבי עקיבא's point depends on the court not having seen the hitting. That suggests that if the judges had seen it, they could judge it themselves, which would mean a witness can become a judge.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it so that...? (opens a question that expects the answer 'no')
Thigh or leg, a less dangerous place to be hit
The lobe of the heart, a very dangerous place to be hit

steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא never says outright that a witness can be a judge. The challenge comes from what his words seem to imply: 'the court didn't see it' suggests that if they had seen it, they could rule.
steps.whyThisMatters: This hidden implication is what makes the ברייתא a challenge to the earlier explanation that רבי עקיבא holds אין עד נעשה דיין.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him:
But did he hit him in front of the court,
so that they know how hard he hit him,
and on what part he hit him –
whether on his thigh
or on the lobe of his heart?
phrases.notes: He means the court has to trust witnesses about the hitting anyway, since the judges weren't there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: וְכִי בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין הִכָּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי עקיבא answers שמעון התימני, and his answer is the source of the challenge in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמעון התימני's rule that the object used to hit must be available for the court itself to inspect.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The court never sees the hitting itself; it already relies on witnesses for how hard and where he hit. So it can also rely on witnesses about the object, and does not need to inspect it.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: the court cannot inspect a building
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא adds that the court cannot check a building someone was pushed from, especially if it collapsed, so it must rely on witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, if someone pushed his friend off the top of a roof or a building and he died, does the court go to the building, or does the building come to the court? And furthermore, if the building fell down, do we rebuild it?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא continues to argue against שמעון התימני. He shows that the court sometimes cannot inspect the thing that caused the harm, so it must trust the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A building cannot be brought to court, and if it collapsed it cannot be checked at all. Still, a person who pushes someone off a roof can be judged. So the court does not need to inspect the weapon itself; the witnesses' testimony is enough.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי עקיבא holds that the court can rely on witnesses about the weapon and how the harm happened. The way he argued suggests that if judges had seen it, they could rule themselves, and that is why the גמרא questions whether he holds אין עד נעשה דיין.

phrases.english: And furthermore, if one pushed his friend
from the top of the roof
or from the top of a building, and he died –
does the court go to the building,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בִירָה הוֹלֶכֶת אֵצֶל בֵּית דִּין?
phrases.english: or does the building go to the court?
phrases.notes: The answer is neither, so the court has to rely on what the witnesses say.

phrases.english: And furthermore, if it fell down,
does one go back and rebuild it?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד, הֲרֵי שֶׁדָּחַף אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ מֵרֹאשׁ הַגָּג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more arguments from רבי עקיבא against שמעון התימני, still inside the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמעון התימני's rule that the object used to cause the harm must be available for the court to inspect.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A building cannot be brought to court, and a collapsed building cannot be checked at all, yet the pusher is still judged. So the court must be able to rely on witnesses.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא's own reading of 'fist'
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא learns from 'fist' that the object only needs to be seen by the witnesses. If the stone is lost and even the witnesses could not see it, the hitter is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, just as a fist is special because witnesses can see it and testify about it, so too anything witnesses can testify about counts. This excludes a case where the stone left the hitter's hand and was lost. There he is פטור.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with רבי עקיבא giving his own explanation of the word 'fist', in place of שמעון התימני's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמעון התימני said the court itself must be able to examine the object. רבי עקיבא changes the requirement: it is enough that the witnesses saw the object and can describe it. Only when even the witnesses could not see it, as with a lost stone, is the hitter פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Fist. The word in the פסוק that both sides are reading.
Handed over to the witnesses, meaning the witnesses could see and assess it
To exclude; this teaches a case that is left out

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי עקיבא, the witnesses are enough to judge the object used to hit. The court does not need to see it.

phrases.english: Rather, just as a fist is special
phrases.notes: This is רבי עקיבא speaking, giving his own reading in place of שמעון התימני's.

phrases.english: in that it is handed over to the witnesses,
so too anything that is handed over to the witnesses;
to exclude when a stone went out
from under the hand of the hitter: he is exempt.
phrases.notes: The stone got lost, so even the witnesses could not see what it was like.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מָה אֶגְרוֹף מְיוּחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting שמעון התימני's reading in Steps 18-19, רבי עקיבא gives his own.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any object the witnesses could assess is enough to make the hitter liable. If even the witnesses could not see it, he is פטור.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא's words seem to allow a witness to be a judge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws an inference from רבי עקיבא's question: if the court did see the hitting, it could judge. That means עד נעשה דיין, which contradicts his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא says that רבי עקיבא told him: 'Did he hit him in front of the court, so that they would know how hard he hit?' This implies that if he did hit him in front of them, they could judge it. So a witness can become a judge!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to its question from Step 16. It uses רבי עקיבא's own words to show he seems to hold that a witness can become a judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא's complaint was only that the court was not present. That suggests that if the judges had seen the hitting, they could rule on it from what they saw. Judging from what you yourself witnessed is עד נעשה דיין, which רבי עקיבא elsewhere rejects.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, it teaches. This signals that the גמרא is pulling out the part of a source it needs.
This implies; it introduces an inference
A witness can become a judge

steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא never says outright that a witness can be a judge. The גמרא is only reading that into his words.

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
Rabbi Akiva said to him:
Did he hit him in front of the court,
so that they would know how hard he hit him?
phrases.notes: These are the words of רבי עקיבא already quoted back in Step 18.

phrases.english: This implies that if he hit him in front of them,
a witness can become a judge!

steps.triggerLanguage: קָתָנֵי מִיהַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the ברייתא fully quoted, the גמרא now uses it for the question raised in Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי עקיבא holds אין עד נעשה דיין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His objection depends only on the court being absent. So if the court were present, its judges could judge from what they saw. That means עד נעשה דיין.

steps.title: He was arguing according to שמעון התימני
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא was only arguing within שמעון התימני's view. He himself does not agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said it according to the words of שמעון התימני, but he himself does not hold that way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: רבי עקיבא's words do not show his own opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמעון התימני wanted the court to examine things itself. רבי עקיבא answered him on his own terms: 'even by your logic, the court usually wasn't there.' This does not mean רבי עקיבא agrees that seeing it would let the judges rule, so he can still hold אין עד נעשה דיין.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the words of; arguing within someone else's view
But he himself does not hold that way

steps.whatToRemember: A rabbi's argument against someone may be made 'within the other side's view'. You cannot always learn his own opinion from it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This removes the contradiction, so רבי עקיבא can consistently hold אין עד נעשה דיין.

phrases.english: He was speaking according to the words of Shimon HaTimni,
but he himself does not hold that way.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִדְבָרָיו דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הַתִּימְנִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Arguing within the other side's view (לדבריו)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא's words show that he lets a witness become a judge.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was only answering שמעון התימני by that sage's own logic. He himself still holds אין עד נעשה דיין.

steps.title: An innocuous ox that killed and damaged gets only a capital trial
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a שור תם that killed a person and then caused damage is judged only with דיני נפשות, not with דיני ממונות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: If a תם ox killed a person and also caused damage, the court judges it with capital law, and does not judge it with monetary law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a ברייתא about an ox that both killed a person and caused damage. This line covers the שור תם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox can face two different court cases: a capital case, where the ox itself is sentenced to death, and a money case, where its owner pays for the damage. For a שור תם, the ברייתא says only the capital case happens. The damage case is dropped.

keyTerms.meaning: An 'innocuous' ox that has not established a pattern of goring.
Capital law, a case that can end in a death sentence.
Monetary law, a case about paying for damage.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
An innocuous ox that killed and caused damage:
phrases.notes: First it killed a person, and after that it went and damaged something.

phrases.english: they judge it with capital law,
and they do not judge it with monetary law.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שׁוֹר תָּם שֶׁהֵמִית וְהִזִּיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a related new ברייתא after the discussion of רבי עקיבא and שמעון התימני.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שור תם that killed and then damaged gets דיני נפשות only, with no monetary trial.

steps.title: A forewarned ox gets a money trial first, then a capital trial
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. A שור מועד that killed and damaged is first judged with דיני ממונות and then with דיני נפשות. If the capital trial came first, the court does not go back to the money trial.
steps.simpleTranslation: A מועד ox that killed and caused damage: the court judges it with monetary law, and then goes back and judges it with capital law. If they judged it with capital law first, they do not go back and judge it with monetary law.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives the rule for a שור מועד, which is different from the תם. It also adds what happens if the court does the trials in the opposite order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a מועד, both trials can happen, but only in one order: money first, then death. If the court ran the capital trial first, the money trial is lost. This last rule is what the גמרא will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'forewarned' ox that has an established pattern of goring.
They go back and judge it again.
They went ahead and judged it first.

phrases.english: A forewarned ox that killed and caused damage:
they judge it with monetary law,
and then go back and judge it with capital law.
If they went ahead and judged it first with capital law,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין חוֹזְרִין וְדָנִין אוֹתוֹ דִּינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת.
phrases.english: they do not go back and judge it with monetary law.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוּעָד שֶׁהֵמִית וְהִזִּיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, moving from the תם case to the מועד case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a מועד, the money trial comes first and the capital trial follows. If the capital trial came first, there is no money trial afterward.

steps.title: Why can't the court go back to the money trial?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the last rule of the ברייתא. Even if the capital trial came first, why not hold the money trial afterward?
steps.simpleTranslation: If they went ahead and judged it first with capital law, so what? Let them go back and judge it with monetary law too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the ברייתא's ruling that after a capital trial the court cannot go back and hold a money trial for a מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already allows both trials for a מועד when the money trial comes first. So the order seems like it should not matter. The גמרא wants to know what stops the court from doing the money trial afterward.

keyTerms.meaning: Let them go back and judge it.

phrases.english: And if they went ahead and judged it first with capital law,
what of it?
Let them go back and judge it with monetary law too!
phrases.notes: Some versions say נָמֵי, 'also', and some say דִּינֵי, 'law of'. Either way, the meaning is the same.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי קָדְמוּ וְדָנוּהוּ דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת מַאי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the final clause of the ברייתא in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that after a capital trial, the court does not go back to judge a מועד with monetary law.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both trials are allowed for a מועד in the other order. The order should not cancel the owner's duty to pay.

steps.title: רבא: the ברייתא follows רבי שמעון התימני
steps.stepSummary: רבא reports that the רבנן of רב's study hall explained that the ברייתא follows רבי שמעון התימני, who compares every case to a fist, which is presented to the court and to the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: I found the Sages of the school of רב sitting and saying: Whose opinion is this? It is רבי שמעון התימני, who said: 'Just as a fist is special in that it is presented to the court and to the witnesses...'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא begins answering the question by saying whose opinion the ברייתא follows. The explanation continues on the next amud, so this line sets up the answer that the גמרא finishes there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון התימני holds that the court rules only when the object involved can be brought before both the judges and the witnesses, like a fist. By naming him, the גמרא hints that the money trial depends on the ox being available to the court. The full reason the court cannot go back after a death sentence comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages of the study hall of רב.
'Whose view is this?' This asks which תנא a teaching follows.
Presented to the court (to judge it) and to the witnesses (to identify it).

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר רָבָא: אַשְׁכַּחְתִּינְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן דְּבֵי רַב,
phrases.english: Rava said: I found the Sages of the school of Rav
who were sitting and saying:

phrases.aramaic: הָא מַנִּי – רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הַתִּימְנִי הִיא,
phrases.english: Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Shimon HaTimni,
who said: 'Just as a fist is special
in that it is presented to the court and to the witnesses,'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר רָבָא: אַשְׁכַּחְתִּינְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן דְּבֵי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the answer to the question in step 25 by naming the תנא whose view the ברייתא follows.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the ברייתא to a specific תנא (רבי שמעון התימני).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The order of the trials should not matter, so the money trial could follow the capital trial.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows רבי שמעון התימני's rule that the object must be presented to the court and witnesses. The full reasoning continues in the next lines.
